title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook: Game Days, Runbooks, and Communications
author: Ava Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose
- This playbook defines Redwood Inference's standard on-call and incident response practices with focused sections for incident lifecycle, runbook templates, on-call rotations, game-day exercises, postmortem process, and customer/status communications. The goal is to ensure consistent, timely responses that meet our SLOs and provide clear customer-facing status updates.

Scope
- Applies to all production services managed by the Platform, Serving Runtime, and SRE teams.
- Includes hosted API, Dedicated, and Private control plane services.

Incident lifecycle (high level)
1. Detection and Triage
   - Alerts originate from telemetry (SLO breaches), health checks, or customer reports.
   - PagerDuty triggers primary on-call for the owning service.
2. Acknowledge & Assess
   - Acknowledge the pager within 5 minutes for Sev1, 15 minutes for Sev2.
   - Initial assesment: scope (customers impacted), impact (functionality, data loss), and ETA for mitigation.
3. Mitigation
   - Apply the owning service runbook checklist (see Runbook Templates below).
   - Use pre-approved remediation steps (rollbacks, config toggles, routing changes).
4. Communicate
   - Internal: update the incident channel (Slack #incidents/<service>) and on-call lead.
   - External: update status.redwood.ai and send customer comms for Sev1/Sev2 (templates below).
5. Post-incident
   - Create a postmortem within 72 hours (initial draft) and complete within 7 days for Sev1.
   - Link postmortem in the incident ticket and update runbooks with lessons learned.

Roles & responsibilities
- Primary On-call (Owner): first responder; executes runbook steps and mitigations.
- Secondary On-call (Backup): supports escalation and takes ownership if Owner is unavailable.
- Incident Commander (IC): appointed when incident escalates to Sev1; coordinates cross-team activity and communications.
- Communications Lead: owns status page updates and customer comms.
- Postmortem Owner: authors the incident report and coordinates reviewers.

Severity definitions and SLO targets
- Sev1 (Critical): widespread outage or data loss affecting >30% of customers or major revenue paths. Response target: page acknowledged <5 minutes; restore or mitigation path within 60 minutes.
- Sev2 (High): partial degradation or subset of customers impacted. Response target: acknowledge <15 minutes; mitigation within 4 hours.
- Sev3 (Medium): minor impact, degraded performance for small cohort. Response target: acknowledge <60 minutes; remediation in next maintenance window.

Escalation matrix (summary)
- On-call Owner -> Secondary (15 min) -> IC -> Team lead -> Eng SRE Pager (after 60 min unresolved for Sev1).
- For security-related incidents escalate directly to Security on-call and legal per policy.

Runbook templates (service-level)
Each service must maintain a runbook with the following sections. Use the checklist items during incident response.
- Service name: plain text
- Owner: team and primary on-call alias
- Pager logic: metrics and thresholds that trigger pages
- Impact assessment checklist: signs of user-facing degradation
- Mitigation steps (ordered)
  1. Verify alert and collect logs (commands below).
  2. Determine if recent deploy or config change coincides with incident.
  3. Roll back last deploy to stable (if safe).
  4. Scale up pods / GPU pool or switch routing to fallback model variant.
  5. Temporarily disable non-critical features (cache warming, batched jobs) to reduce load.
  6. Engage infra team for hardware/network faults.
- Post-mitigation validation: smoke tests and key metric checks.
- Rollback and recovery commands (examples):
  - kubectl -n serving get pods -l app=<service>
  - kubectl -n serving logs <pod> --since=10m --tail=200
  - ./infra/scripts/adjust-gpu-pool --scale-to 8 --region us-west1
  - curl -sS https://localhost:8080/health | jq '.'

Runbook example checklist (Embedding service)
- Alert: embedding latency > 500ms p95 for 5m or error rate > 1%
- Quick checks:
  - Confirm metrics in Grafana dashboard "embedding/latency"
  - Check recent model rollout (last 24h)
  - Verify GPU utilization and OOM events
- Mitigations:
  1. Revert to quantization-profile v1.2 if rollout in last 24h.
  2. Increase batch window from 20ms to 50ms for spikes.
  3. Fall back to cached embeddings for known keys.

Game days (exercise program)
Purpose
- Validate runbooks, on-call rotations, and communications under controlled failure scenarios. Game days ensure that playbooks remain actionable and that SLOs/alerts are tuned correctly.
Frequency & ownership
- Quarterly platform-wide game day (SRE lead).
- Monthly team-level tabletop exercises (service owners).
- Every on-call rotation includes one simulated incident run.
Types of exercises
1. Live failure injection (controlled Chaos): e.g., simulate a GPU node failure or increased tail latency from model runtime.
2. Tabletop: scenario walkthrough without production changes (use for new hires).
3. Blackout: simulate monitoring outage and rely on synthetic transactions and customer reports.
Game day checklist
- Pre-game: identify scope, safe rollback mechanisms, and a kill-switch owner.
- During game: track time-to-detect, time-to-ack, time-to-mitigate, and communication cadence.
- Post-game: write a short retro and update runbooks/alerts. Each exercise must include at least one corrective action with an assigned owner and completion date.

Incident communication templates
- Internal Slack (initial):
  "[INCIDENT] <Service> - <Sev> detected at <HH:MM UTC>. Impact: <short summary>. Owner: @<oncall>. Working: initial triage in progress. Will update every 15 minutes."
- Status page update (public):
  Title: " degraded performance for <service>"
  Body: "We are investigating reports of degraded performance for <service>. Some customers may see increased latency or errors. Our on-call team is actively working on mitigation. We will provide updates every 30 minutes. Affected regions: <regions>."
- Customer email (Sev1 template):
  Subject: "Incident impacting <service> - <start time UTC>"
  Body: "Hello,\n\nWe experienced an incident starting at <time UTC> impacting <service> which may have affected your requests. Our engineering team identified the root cause and applied a mitigation at <time>. We are following up with a postmortem and will notify you when it is published. If you need immediate assistance, contact your CSM or support@redwood.ai.\n\nWe apologize for the disruption.\n- Redwood Inference Support"

Postmortem process (standard)
- Trigger: any Sev1 incident; Sev2 incidents when customer-impacting or recurring.
- Timeline:
  1. Create an incident doc (Confluence) within 72 hours with timeline and preliminary impact.
  2. Postmortem draft due in 7 days; reviewers assigned (IC, team lead, SRE).
  3. Final postmortem published and retro held within 14 days.
- Required sections:
  - Summary and impact (customer count, duration, revenue impact if known)
  - Timeline of events with timestamps and actors
  - Root cause analysis (RCA) and contributing factors
  - Corrective actions (owner and due date)
  - Changes to monitoring/runbooks/alerts and verification plan

Metrics & dashboards to maintain
- SLOs: request latency (p95/p99), error rate (5m), availability by region.
- Dashboards (examples): "platform/availability", "serving/latency-by-model", "gpu-fleet/usage-and-oom".
- Game-day metrics to record: time-to-detect, ack, mitigate, and customer-impact window.

Templates & artifacts (checklist)
- Incident Slack channel template: #incident-<service>-YYYYMMDD
- Incident Confluence template: use "Incident - Postmortem Template v2" (link in related_pages)
- Status page template snippet: stored in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/status-page-templates
- PagerDuty escalation policy per service: reference policy id in runbook.

Operational expectations and hygiene
- Keep runbooks current: runbooks must be reviewed after any incident and at least quarterly.
- On-call rotation signups: rotations published 6 weeks in advance.
- Coverage: each service must have primary and secondary on-call aliases and documented handoff steps.

Appendix A: Quick comms templates
- Slack follow-up update: "Update: Mitigation applied at <time>. Error rate reduced from X% -> Y%. Working on full recovery and root cause. Next update in 30 minutes."
- Final customer update: "We resolved the incident at <time>. Root cause: <short RCA>. Corrective actions: <list>. Postmortem: <link>."

Appendix B: Sample runbook header (text table)
- Service | Owner | Pager Alias | Primary Metrics | Runbook Link
- embedding-service | Platform Team | @pd-embedding | p95_latency, error_rate | /confluence/embedding-runbook

Appendix C: Game day report checklist
- Scenario name
- Date/time
- Participants
- Detection method (alert/manual/customer)
- Timings: detect/ack/mitigate/recover
- Observations and corrective actions

How to use this playbook
- Follow runbooks first; escalate to IC for Sev1s. Use game days to validate process. Keep communications factual and timely. Postmortems drive continuous improvement and must include owners and due dates for corrective actions.

Ownership and feedback
- Playbook owner: Eng SRE (sre-lead@redwood.ai).
- For updates or feedback, open a PR on the Confluence source or contact the playbook owner.
summary: Comprehensive playbook covering incident lifecycle, runbooks, on-call rotations, game days, communications, and postmortem process for Redwood Inference.
